scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

The effectiveness of Yom Kippur depends on how individuals integrate its lessons into daily life. If approached with genuine commitment, it can be transformative, fostering a mindful and intentional approach to actions and relationships throughout the year. Thus, Yom Kippur can indeed change how seriously people take their mistakes, encouraging a more thoughtful and proactive stance in their lives.

When we're out with my friends or just hanging out, she talks about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, all the vacations she takes, how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie and came back to work a little later. She replied, "Yeah, but I can set my own hours." That rubbed me the wrong way, and I told her she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks because it was obnoxious and came off as braggy. She said she was just explaining something, and I said it wasn't just this one thingâĢĶit was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives. She said she's where she is because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked hard, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. Instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it and stormed off. So, am I being unreasonable (AITA) for what I said? First, I need to understand why I'm feeling this way. It seems like I'm frustrated because her job is so different from what most people have, and she's constantly talking about it. Maybe I feel like she's bragging or showing off, which makes me uncomfortable, especially around our friends who might not have the same opportunities. On the other hand, she's proud of her job and the opportunities she has. She worked hard to get there, and she's entitled to talk about her achievements. Maybe I'm being too sensitive or jealous, as she suggested. I also need to consider how our relationship is affected by this. If I'm constantly frustrated with her talking about her job, it could lead to more arguments or tension between us. It's important to communicate my feelings without making her feel attacked or defensive. Perhaps I should think about why her job perks bother me so much. Is it because I feel like I don't have the same opportunities, or is it because I'm worried about how others perceive us? Understanding my own feelings could help me address the issue more constructively. I also need to consider her perspective. She's proud of her job and the work-life balance she's achieved. She might not realize how her constant talking about it affects me, especially in social settings. Maybe she doesn't see it as bragging but just sharing her positive experiences. It's also possible that I'm projecting my own insecurities onto her. If I'm feeling unfulfilled or envious of her job, that could be influencing how I react to her talking about it. It might be helpful to reflect on my own feelings and goals to address any underlying issues. In terms of communication, I should approach this conversation with empathy and understanding. Instead of accusing her of bragging, I could express how her constant talking about her job makes me feel and why it's important to me to have a more balanced conversation. I should also acknowledge her achievements and express pride in her success. This way, she feels appreciated and understood, which can help reduce defensiveness and open up a more constructive dialogue. Maybe setting some boundaries or agreeing on how often to discuss her job could help. For example, we could agree to limit conversations about her job in social settings or find a way to balance the topics we discuss. It's also important to recognize that everyone has different ways of expressing pride in their work. What might seem like bragging to me could just be her way of sharing her joy and satisfaction in her job. Understanding and respecting her communication style, while also expressing my needs, is key to resolving this issue. In summary, I need to reflect on why her job perks bother me, communicate my feelings constructively, acknowledge her achievements, and work together to find a balance that respects both of our perspectives.
